html:
The Sasanian Empire was the last Iranian empire before Islam, ruled by the House of Sasan from 224 to 651 CE. Its people called it Eranshahr, "the land of the Iranians". For four centuries it was the great rival of Rome and then of the Eastern Roman Empire.

Ardashir I, a king in Persis in south-west Iran, overthrew the Parthian Empire in 224 CE. The Sasanians ruled from Ctesiphon in Mesopotamia and built a more centralised state than the Parthians had.

Highlights:

  • Shapur I won great victories over Rome and in 260 CE captured the emperor Valerian, a scene carved in rock reliefs in Iran.
  • Zoroastrianism became the state religion, with a powerful priesthood. The prophet Mani founded Manichaeism here and was put to death.
  • Khosrow I (531 to 579) reformed taxes and the army, and his court welcomed scholars, including Greek philosophers driven out of Athens.

Sasanian art, silverwork and court life were admired from Rome to China. Games like chess and polo were popular at court.

Wars with Rome came again and again, including the war of 572 to 591. The last and greatest began in 602. Khosrow II took Syria, Palestine and Egypt, but the Roman emperor Heraclius struck back into Iran, and Khosrow was overthrown in 628.

Both empires were left exhausted, just as the Arabs united under Islam. In the Arab conquests Muslim armies took Mesopotamia and then Iran, and the last king, Yazdegerd III, was killed in 651. Persian culture lived on inside the Islamic world.
